flashcards.q: State the protobuf tag formula and decode tag byte 0x08.
flashcards.a: tag = (field_number << 3) | wire_type. 0x08 = binary 0000 1000 -> wire_type = last 3 bits = 0 (varint), field_number = remaining bits shifted right 3 = 1. So 0x08 is field 1, varint wire type.

flashcards.q: Encode int32 field 1 = 150 in protobuf wire format.
flashcards.a: Tag = (1<<3)|0 = 0x08. Value 150 as varint (7 bits/byte, MSB=continuation, little-endian groups) = 0x96 0x01 (two bytes since 150 needs more than 7 bits). Full encoding: 08 96 01 (3 bytes total).

flashcards.q: List the 4 protobuf wire types and what they encode.
flashcards.a: 0 = varint (int32/int64/bool/enum), 1 = 64-bit fixed, 2 = length-delimited (string/bytes/embedded message/packed repeated), 5 = 32-bit fixed.

flashcards.q: What protobuf schema change silently corrupts data with no error thrown?
flashcards.a: Reusing a field number for a different field after it was previously used and removed. An old message deserialized with the new field's meaning applied to old bytes produces wrong data silently -- nothing crashes because the parser doesn't validate a field number's historical meaning.

flashcards.q: Why does gRPC require HTTP/2 and cannot run on HTTP/1.1?
flashcards.a: gRPC needs trailing headers (HTTP/2 trailers frame) to carry the final grpc-status after the body since the outcome isn't known until the handler finishes, and it needs true independent multiplexed streams for concurrent RPCs plus native bidirectional streaming -- neither reliably exists on HTTP/1.1.

flashcards.q: Name the 4 gRPC RPC types and a use case for each.
flashcards.a: Unary (fetch-a-record). Server-streaming (log tail, live price feed -- 1 request, N responses). Client-streaming (chunked upload, batched telemetry with one final ack -- N requests, 1 response). Bidirectional streaming (chat-like, live audio-to-text -- N and M interleaved, independently paced).

flashcards.q: How does a gRPC deadline differ from a plain per-call timeout?
flashcards.a: A deadline is an absolute timestamp set once by the originating client and auto-propagated through every downstream call derived from that request's context. A per-call timeout is independently set at each hop with no shared knowledge -- so uncoordinated hop timeouts can collectively blow past what the original caller wanted.

flashcards.q: What happens to child RPCs when a parent gRPC context is cancelled?
flashcards.a: Cancelling the parent context cancels every child call derived from it, so downstream services stop doing work nobody's waiting on -- this only works if downstream calls actually derive their context from the inbound one; a fresh/unrelated context silently breaks propagation.

flashcards.q: List gRPC's status code count and 5 key codes with their meaning.
flashcards.a: 17 total codes including OK. Key ones: CANCELLED (client cancelled), DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (ran out of time), INVALID_ARGUMENT (client sent bad request, don't retry), UNAVAILABLE (transient, retry may help), FAILED_PRECONDITION (client must fix state before retrying, don't blindly retry).

flashcards.q: What does google.rpc.Status give you beyond a bare status code?
flashcards.a: Structured, typed error `details` (e.g. a BadRequest message listing which fields violated validation, or RetryInfo suggesting a backoff duration) so a client can programmatically branch on rich error content instead of parsing a human-readable message string.

flashcards.q: What is a gRPC interceptor, and where does auth validation belong?
flashcards.a: Middleware wrapping every RPC -- client-side interceptors wrap outgoing calls (inject auth, tracing), server-side wrap incoming calls (validate auth, rate-limit, metrics), composed in a chain analogous to HTTP middleware. Auth belongs in a server-side interceptor, not duplicated in every service method.

flashcards.q: When does gRPC beat REST, and when does REST win?
flashcards.a: gRPC wins for internal service-to-service calls needing low latency, strict schemas, streaming, and polyglot codegen. REST wins for public/third-party APIs and browser clients: curl-ability, standard HTTP caching (ETag/Cache-Control), and no proxy requirement (gRPC-Web needs Envoy or similar to reach browsers directly).

flashcards.q: What's the operational gotcha with load balancing gRPC traffic?
flashcards.a: gRPC keeps a single long-lived HTTP/2 connection per client-server pair. A plain L4/TCP load balancer only balances new CONNECTIONS, not requests within one -- one backend pod can get all the traffic while others sit idle. Fix: client-side load balancing or an L7-aware proxy (Envoy) that balances individual streams.
